1) [Se'if 1] One should be careful to kasher with boiling water, etc. The procedure is as follows. One takes a large cauldron filled with water and brings it to a vigorous boil, until the boiling water reaches every surface of the cauldron, inside and out. One places into it all the utensils one wishes to kasher, inserting them individually, one after another. Levush. Regarding a large utensil that cannot be inserted into the cauldron, see below, se'if 6.
2) Regarding how long a utensil must remain in the cauldron during kashering, Rif in the chapter Kol Sha'ah writes that it should remain there until it expels what it absorbed. Ran writes likewise there, as do Rambam, chapter 5, halachah 23; Raavad in Sefer Tamim De'im, siman 25; and Rashba in Toras HaBayis, bayis 4, sha'ar 4. Radbaz in Leshonos HaRambam, siman 241, demonstrates that this is Rambam's view. See there. Tur, however, writes that the custom is to insert the utensils and remove them immediately. He writes likewise in Yoreh De'ah, siman 121. See there. Mordechai, chapter Kol Sha'ah, siman 579, writes likewise, as cited by Beis Yosef. Levush, se'if 2, also writes likewise. Peri Chadash, at the end of se'if 6, writes that the Jewish people's custom has the force of Torah. Taz, subsection 2, however, writes that Tur's statement to remove them 'immediately' is not literal; they must remain at least briefly. Kol Bo likewise writes that one must be careful not to hurry to remove a utensil from the cauldron, allowing time for the boiling water to enter it and extract what it absorbed. Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 1; Shulchan Aruch HaRav, subsection 4; Ben Ish Chai, parashas Tzav, subsection 12, write likewise. See below, subsection 14.
3) One might ask: According to the opinion that intentionally nullifying a prohibition is forbidden under Torah law, how did the Torah permit kashering the utensils of Midian with boiling water? This appears to intentionally nullify the prohibition absorbed in them within the kashering water. The answer is that the rule against intentionally nullifying a prohibition applies only when one intends to mix a prohibited substance into permitted food in order to benefit from it. Here, one intends to kasher the utensil and derives no benefit from the prohibited substance, so it is permitted. Ran, chapter Ein Ma'amidin.
4) There. Before the fifth hour. At that time there is a secondary transfer of permitted flavor. Beis Yosef; Taz, subsection 1. How does this occur? The chametz imparts flavor to the utensil, the utensil imparts flavor to the water, and the water then imparts flavor back into the bowl, while the prohibition of chametz has not yet taken effect. Mordechai, chapter Kol Sha'ah, siman 576; Levush, se'if 3. Although some maintain that since it retains the designation chametz, it is considered to have absorbed a prohibited substance, and Maran took their view into account above in siman 451, se'if 4, here he relies upon the lenient authorities because some authorities independently permit all these matters. Ma'amar Mordechai, subsection 1. See above, siman 451, subsection 39.
5) There. Before the fifth hour. This means before the beginning of the fifth hour, namely, by the end of the fourth hour. Since chametz is at least rabbinically prohibited from the fifth hour, as stated above at the beginning of siman 443, its flavor is no longer considered a secondary transfer of permitted flavor. Peri Chadash; Mateh Yehudah; Mekor Chaim, subsection 1; Nehar Shalom, subsection 1; Shulchan Aruch HaRav, subsection 8; Chayei Adam, rule 125, subsection 33.
6) There. So that one will not need, etc. At that time, one need not ensure that the utensil was not used that day. Even if it was used that day and the water does not equal sixty times the utensils, it is permitted, because chametz is still permitted and this is a secondary transfer of permitted flavor. Tosafos, Chullin 108b and Avodah Zarah 76a; Rosh at the end of Avodah Zarah and in the chapter Kol Sha'ah; Mordechai, chapter Kol Sha'ah; Ran at the end of the chapter Kol HaBasar. Tur and Beis Yosef cite these authorities. Olas Shabbos, subsection 1; Magen Avraham, subsection 1; Chok Yaakov, subsection 2; Chok Yosef, subsection 1; Mekor Chaim, subsection 2; Shulchan Aruch HaRav, subsection 13; Chayei Adam, there, subsection 33, write likewise. Although the gloss above in siman 447, se'if 5, prohibits foods cooked in a chametz utensil and does not permit them because of a secondary transfer of flavor, here there are several successive transfers: from the food to the utensil, from the utensil to the water, and from the water to the second utensil. It is therefore permitted. Magen Avraham, there; Chok Yaakov, there; Mekor Chaim, there. All this is the strict law, but the custom is not to kasher any utensil that was used that day, as stated below in the gloss to se'if 2. See there. See also below, subsection 21, regarding whether the cauldron used for kashering must first itself be kashered.
7) An incident occurred in which a piece of bread was found in the cauldron used to kasher utensils before Pesach. The question was whether the utensils had to be kashered a second time. Beis David, siman 195, concludes that according to communities that do not apply the rule that a piece becomes intrinsically prohibited, it is obvious that the utensils are not prohibited, because the flavor expelled from the bread into the water was nullified in sixty. Even according to communities that do apply that rule, a second kashering is unnecessary. Their acceptance of the rule was observed only regarding a tangible substance, not mere flavor. Although they customarily kasher kneading utensils belonging to lenient communities, and so forth, that is only an initial stringency. Since this is a custom, we should not add further stringency. If it is clearly established, however, that their custom is to prohibit even after the fact because of flavor alone, then these utensils must certainly be kashered again. See there. Zechor LeAvraham, at the end of siman 451. See above, siman 447, subsections 59 and 76.

cases.en_plain: 1) [Se'if 1] One should be careful to kasher with boiling water, etc. The procedure is as follows. One takes a large cauldron filled with water and brings it to a vigorous boil, until the boiling water reaches every surface of the cauldron, inside and out. One places into it all the utensils one wishes to kasher, inserting them individually, one after another. Levush. Regarding a large utensil that cannot be inserted into the cauldron, see below, se'if 6. 2) Regarding how long a utensil must remain in the cauldron during kashering, Rif in the chapter Kol Sha'ah writes that it should remain there until it expels what it absorbed. Ran writes likewise there, as do Rambam, chapter 5, halachah 23; Raavad in Sefer Tamim De'im, siman 25; and Rashba in Toras HaBayis, bayis 4, sha'ar 4. Radbaz in Leshonos HaRambam, siman 241, demonstrates that this is Rambam's view. See there. Tur, however, writes that the custom is to insert the utensils and remove them immediately. He writes likewise in Yoreh De'ah, siman 121. See there. Mordechai, chapter Kol Sha'ah, siman 579, writes likewise, as cited by Beis Yosef. Levush, se'if 2, also writes likewise. Peri Chadash, at the end of se'if 6, writes that the Jewish people's custom has the force of Torah. Taz, subsection 2, however, writes that Tur's statement to remove them 'immediately' is not literal; they must remain at least briefly. Kol Bo likewise writes that one must be careful not to hurry to remove a utensil from the cauldron, allowing time for the boiling water to enter it and extract what it absorbed. Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 1; Shulchan Aruch HaRav, subsection 4; Ben Ish Chai, parashas Tzav, subsection 12, write likewise. See below, subsection 14. 3) One might ask: According to the opinion that intentionally nullifying a prohibition is forbidden under Torah law, how did the Torah permit kashering the utensils of Midian with boiling water? This appears to intentionally nullify the prohibition absorbed in them within the kashering water. The answer is that the rule against intentionally nullifying a prohibition applies only when one intends to mix a prohibited substance into permitted food in order to benefit from it. Here, one intends to kasher the utensil and derives no benefit from the prohibited substance, so it is permitted. Ran, chapter Ein Ma'amidin. 4) There. Before the fifth hour. At that time there is a secondary transfer of permitted flavor. Beis Yosef; Taz, subsection 1. How does this occur? The chametz imparts flavor to the utensil, the utensil imparts flavor to the water, and the water then imparts flavor back into the bowl, while the prohibition of chametz has not yet taken effect. Mordechai, chapter Kol Sha'ah, siman 576; Levush, se'if 3. Although some maintain that since it retains the designation chametz, it is considered to have absorbed a prohibited substance, and Maran took their view into account above in siman 451, se'if 4, here he relies upon the lenient authorities because some authorities independently permit all these matters. Ma'amar Mordechai, subsection 1. See above, siman 451, subsection 39. 5) There. Before the fifth hour. This means before the beginning of the fifth hour, namely, by the end of the fourth hour. Since chametz is at least rabbinically prohibited from the fifth hour, as stated above at the beginning of siman 443, its flavor is no longer considered a secondary transfer of permitted flavor. Peri Chadash; Mateh Yehudah; Mekor Chaim, subsection 1; Nehar Shalom, subsection 1; Shulchan Aruch HaRav, subsection 8; Chayei Adam, rule 125, subsection 33. 6) There. So that one will not need, etc. At that time, one need not ensure that the utensil was not used that day. Even if it was used that day and the water does not equal sixty times the utensils, it is permitted, because chametz is still permitted and this is a secondary transfer of permitted flavor. Tosafos, Chullin 108b and Avodah Zarah 76a; Rosh at the end of Avodah Zarah and in the chapter Kol Sha'ah; Mordechai, chapter Kol Sha'ah; Ran at the end of the chapter Kol HaBasar. Tur and Beis Yosef cite these authorities. Olas Shabbos, subsection 1; Magen Avraham, subsection 1; Chok Yaakov, subsection 2; Chok Yosef, subsection 1; Mekor Chaim, subsection 2; Shulchan Aruch HaRav, subsection 13; Chayei Adam, there, subsection 33, write likewise. Although the gloss above in siman 447, se'if 5, prohibits foods cooked in a chametz utensil and does not permit them because of a secondary transfer of flavor, here there are several successive transfers: from the food to the utensil, from the utensil to the water, and from the water to the second utensil. It is therefore permitted. Magen Avraham, there; Chok Yaakov, there; Mekor Chaim, there. All this is the strict law, but the custom is not to kasher any utensil that was used that day, as stated below in the gloss to se'if 2. See there. See also below, subsection 21, regarding whether the cauldron used for kashering must first itself be kashered. 7) An incident occurred in which a piece of bread was found in the cauldron used to kasher utensils before Pesach. The question was whether the utensils had to be kashered a second time. Beis David, siman 195, concludes that according to communities that do not apply the rule that a piece becomes intrinsically prohibited, it is obvious that the utensils are not prohibited, because the flavor expelled from the bread into the water was nullified in sixty. Even according to communities that do apply that rule, a second kashering is unnecessary. Their acceptance of the rule was observed only regarding a tangible substance, not mere flavor. Although they customarily kasher kneading utensils belonging to lenient communities, and so forth, that is only an initial stringency. Since this is a custom, we should not add further stringency. If it is clearly established, however, that their custom is to prohibit even after the fact because of flavor alone, then these utensils must certainly be kashered again. See there. Zechor LeAvraham, at the end of siman 451. See above, siman 447, subsections 59 and 76.

If the vessels are ben yomo. For even though the vessel is ben yomo and there is not sixty times [as much] water against it, nevertheless it is permitted, because it is a giving of taste after a giving of taste of what is permitted, which is not so after the fifth hour. And it is difficult: for in siman 447, se'if 5, the Rama forbids things cooked [in such vessels] and did not permit on the grounds of a giving of taste after a giving of taste; so why does he permit here ab initio? One may say that here, since there are many [transfers of] taste from the food to the vessel and from the vessel to the water and from the water to the vessel, it is permitted.
Whose absorption is slight. Such as spoons and cups; and one must be concerned that they will absorb from what the bowls and pots expel.
However, many dispute, etc. The words of the Rama are puzzling, for Beis Yosef also agrees to this; rather, after its prohibition, once the water has ceased boiling it is forbidden to bring it to a boil a second time, for so long as they are boiling they have not absorbed from the hagalah water, and if they ceased boiling they absorbed; but before the time of prohibition it is permitted, for it is a giving of taste after a giving of taste of what is permitted; and so wrote Hagahot Maimoniyot; and so wrote Maharshal in a responsum.
And that one not insert. So that it not absorb from the hagalah water.
At the beginning and at the end. Meaning that it suffices when one does hagalah at the beginning or at the end.
One must be careful in all, etc. Meaning that one should see that the vessels not be ben yomo; and if it is ben yomo, there must be sixty times [as much] water against it; and if one does hagalah for many vessels one after another, there must be sixty against all of them, for the prohibition returns and reawakens (Beis Yosef and Darchei Moshe in the name of the Rashba, siman 262). And it appears to me that if one vessel absorbed meat and the other fish, it does not return and reawaken, since they are distinct tastes, as is written in Yoreh De'ah at the end of siman 98. And one should first do hagalah for vessels whose absorption is slight, and afterward vessels whose absorption is great; and one should not leave them [in] longer than necessary; and the water should not cease boiling; and one does hagalah for the cauldron at the beginning and at the end. It appears to me that if the cauldron is not ben yomo, one need not do hagalah for it at the beginning, for it is no worse than the vessels themselves; and if one did hagalah for it at the beginning, one need not do hagalah for it at the end, for the vessels are not ben yomo; yet the practice is to be stringent with all the stringencies even before the fifth [hour], and so wrote the Bach. And this requires further study: why did the Rama specify after six, for even after four one must be careful, as is written above, for even though it is a rabbinic prohibition, nevertheless a giving of taste after a giving of taste does not apply; see siman 447, se'if 3, that regarding something that has in it only a taste of chametz we do not say it returns and reawakens; not like Olas Shabbos.

ויעלו על שפתו. אבל כלי שתשמישו מבחוץ כמו קערה שכופין לפעמים על הקדרה או כלי ששואבין בה מהקדרה אף צד החיצון בעי הגעלה וכת' המ"א בשם מהרי"ל כלי שפיהו צר שא"א לשפשפו בפנים או שיש לה קנים אסור בהגעלה עכ"ל.

He should form a rim at its mouth with clay. During the rest of the year one may form a rim from dough, as stated in Kol Shaah. Beis Hillel, Yoreh Deah 121, seif katan 1, writes that Rosh in Kol Shaah clearly implies that only regarding chametz for Pesach, where permitted matter was absorbed, is such a rim effective for a large utensil. For other prohibitions, a large utensil must first undergo hagalah once, and afterward a rim is needed for its lip. According to him, this distinction applies only to other prohibitions, whereas for chametz before Pesach a first hagalah is unnecessary before refilling it with boiling water and using the rim. He adds that Rif in chapter 2 of Avodah Zarah, who cites the case of Mar Ukva, does not imply such a distinction. These words are astonishing. Rosh contains no implication whatever supporting such a distinction. His reference to performing hagalah on the cauldron twice concerns a case where utensils are kashered within that cauldron, so the cauldron must undergo hagalah before and after, as the Mechaber wrote above in seif 1. Likewise, the claim regarding Rif is even more difficult, for Rosh also cites that case at the end of HaSocher Es HaPoel. The rule is that there is no distinction at all in this law, except that a dough rim cannot be used during Pesach itself, as is evident from the Gemara and all the authorities.
And the water should rise over its rim. If a utensil is used on its outside, such as a bowl that is sometimes inverted over a pot, or a vessel used to draw food from a pot, its exterior also requires hagalah. Magen Avraham writes in the name of Maharil that a narrow-necked utensil that cannot be scrubbed inside, or a utensil with tubes, cannot be kashered through hagalah.

cases.en_html: 6) There. So that one will not need, etc. At that time, one need not ensure that the utensil was not used that day. Even if it was used that day and the water does not equal sixty times the utensils, it is permitted, because chametz is still permitted and this is a secondary transfer of permitted flavor. Tosafos, Chullin 108b and Avodah Zarah 76a; Rosh at the end of Avodah Zarah and in the chapter Kol Sha'ah; Mordechai, chapter Kol Sha'ah; Ran at the end of the chapter Kol HaBasar. Tur and Beis Yosef cite these authorities. Olas Shabbos, subsection 1; Magen Avraham, subsection 1; Chok Yaakov, subsection 2; Chok Yosef, subsection 1; Mekor Chaim, subsection 2; Shulchan Aruch HaRav, subsection 13; Chayei Adam, there, subsection 33, write likewise. Although the gloss above in siman 447, se'if 5, prohibits foods cooked in a chametz utensil and does not permit them because of a secondary transfer of flavor, here there are several successive transfers: from the food to the utensil, from the utensil to the water, and from the water to the second utensil. It is therefore permitted. Magen Avraham, there; Chok Yaakov, there; Mekor Chaim, there.
